newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO haggle on details as Hebron deal nears.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO haggle on details as Hebron deal nears.

text.p: Israel and the Palestinians haggled over prisoner releases and target dates for future West Bank handovers on Tuesday as the two sides neared a deal on the town of Hebron, PLO negotiators said.

A PLO official said a planned summit between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat would be put off until Wednesday because the Israeli leader was busy with a parliamentary budget debate.
But Israel's Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai told reporters: "I think they are going to meet today and we will see what will happen."

PLO officials said that whenever a summit took place, negotiators could initial the deal giving Palestinians self-rule in 80 percent of the West Bank town. The sides were putting final touches on the accord at a Jerusalem hotel.

"The agreement on Hebron has been concluded. The problem is what comes after Hebron. We are still discussing other outstanding issues such as further redeployments and prisoners," said Major-General Abdel-Razak al-Yahya, a top negotiator.

Palestinians view Israel's release of prisoners as crucial to winning support for peace deals on the Palestinian street. Hebron is the last town due to get self-rule but West Bank rural areas remain on the agenda.
Underscoring tensions in Hebron, Jewish settlers tried to take over a vacant house before dawn in the Arab casbah.
Israeli security forces made 15 arrests, said the settlers, who oppose a handover of any part of the town holy to Moslems and Jews as the burial place of the biblical Abraham.
Under an Israeli-PLO agreement signed in 1995, Hebron was due to have been given self-rule nine months ago. Officials say a handover could be implemented within hours of any deal.

Security issues have delayed the transfer -- first a wave of Islamist suicide bombings in Israel that killed 59 people, and later Netanyahu's demands for better protection for the 400 Jews in the heart of the town of 100,000 Arabs.

U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross, who has pushed and pulled the sides together during three months of negotiations, shuttled between Netanyahu in Jerusalem and Arafat in Gaza hoping to clinch an agreement on Tuesday, PLO officials said.

The Arab world regards Hebron as a test of Netanyahu's intentions. Although opposed to swapping occupied Arab land for peace, the right-wing Likud party leader has promised to uphold the peace deals of the left-leaning government he ousted in May.

Under pressure from Washington, Israel's closest ally, Netanyahu stayed with the negotiations while emphasising that 20 percent of the town, including Hebron's Jews and Abraham's tomb, will remain under Israeli control.

Many of Netanyahu's right-wing followers, including Jewish settlers, view the West Bank as the biblical birthright of Jews -- the Land of Israel promised them by God. Many view Arafat as a terrorist bent on Israel's destruction.

Though at times fiercely defiant, Netanyahu can little afford to ignore the policy concerns of Washington, Israel's crucial ally, which views a Hebron pullback as critical to the future of Middle East peacemaking.

In violence on Monday night, a Gaza Strip settler shot dead a Palestinian who entered the isolated Kfar Darom settlement. A military source said the settler fired when the Palestinian refused an order to stop.
Palestinians, who identified the dead man as 30-year-old Ibrahim Abu Nuseir, demanded a joint investigation.
